claim: The cerebellum has a parasagittal modular architecture characterized by precisely organized climbing fiber (CF) projections that are congruent with alternating aldolase C/zebrin II expression.
source: The cerebellum has a parasagittal modular architecture characterized by precisely organized climbing fiber (CF) projections that are congruent with alternating aldolase C/zebrin II expression.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established anatomical knowledge about cerebellar organization.

claim: CF signals in medial modules show anticipatory decreases, early increases, secondary increases, and reward-related increases or decreases.
source: CF signals in medial modules show anticipatory decreases, early increases, secondary increases, and reward-related increases or decreases, which represent quick motor initiation, go cues, fast motor behavior, and positive reward outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from two-photon calcium imaging during the behavioral task, as shown in multiple figures including Figures 4-7.

claim: CF signals in lateral modules show early increases and reward-related decreases.
source: CF signals in lateral modules show early increases and reward-related decreases, which represent no-go and/or go cues and positive reward outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from two-photon calcium imaging, as shown in Figures 3, 5, and 7.

claim: The boundaries of CF functions broadly correspond to those of aldolase C patterning.
source: The boundaries of CF functions broadly correspond to those of aldolase C patterning.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing response probability across AldC boundaries and Figure 2—figure supplement 2-4 showing clustering analysis.

claim: Spatially segregated CF inputs in different modules play distinct roles in the execution of goal-directed behavior.
source: These results indicate that spatially segregated CF inputs in different modules play distinct roles in the execution of goal-directed behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing different CF signal patterns across modules during the behavioral task.

claim: The inputs and outputs of the cerebellar cortex are organized into modules.
source: The inputs and outputs of the cerebellar cortex are organized into modules (Voogd and Glickstein, 1998), wherein spatially defined populations of Purkinje cells (PCs) project to a distinct subdivision of the cerebellar nucleus, which in turn projects to a subnucleus of the inferior olive that provides climbing fiber (CF) inputs to PCs.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Voogd and Glickstein, 1998.

claim: Each hemi-cerebellum can be subdivided into 14 alternating aldolase C-positive (AldC+) and aldolase C-negative (AldC−) compartments (1+ to 7+).
source: Each hemi-cerebellum can be subdivided into 14 alternating aldolase C-positive (AldC+) and aldolase C-negative (AldC−) compartments (1+ to 7+), which are largely congruent with the classical zones (Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004; Voogd and Ruigrok, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004 and Voogd and Ruigrok, 2004.

claim: AldC+ PCs receive enhanced glutamate release by CFs.
source: AldC+ PCs receive enhanced glutamate release by CFs (Paukert et al., 2010), but parallel fiber inputs that are similar to those received by AldC− PCs (Nguyen-Minh et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Paukert et al., 2010 and Nguyen-Minh et al., 2018.

claim: AldC+ and AldC− PCs show distinct firing properties and plasticity rules.
source: AldC+ and AldC− PCs show distinct firing properties and plasticity rules (Zhou et al., 2014), and differ in interaction between simple and complex spikes (Tang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2014 and Tang et al., 2017.

claim: CF inputs to AldC+ and AldC− compartments are separately and precisely synchronized at cellular resolution.
source: CF inputs to AldC+ and AldC− compartments are separately and precisely synchronized at cellular resolution (Tsutsumi et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tsutsumi et al., 2015.

claim: AldC+ and AldC− PCs respond differently to optic flow stimulation in the pigeon cerebellum.
source: AldC+ and AldC− PCs respond differently to optic flow stimulation in the pigeon cerebellum (Graham and Wylie, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Graham and Wylie, 2012.

claim: Well-trained mice almost completely withheld licking after a no-go cue.
source: Well-trained mice almost completely withheld licking after a no-go cue (Figure 1B) and cut off protracted licking, yielding a constant inter-trial interval (hit, CR, and miss trials: 6.23 ± 0.58 s; FA trials: 10.98 ± 1.65 s; mean ± s.d., n = 17 mice).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B and quantified in the text.

claim: Licking in hit trials was shorter in latency, higher in frequency, longer in duration, and more regular than licking in FA trials.
source: Licking in hit trials was shorter in latency, higher in frequency, longer in duration, and more regular than licking in FA trials (Figure 1C and D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C, D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The performance of mice quickly improved to an expert level, defined as fraction of correct trials >80%, within 3–6 sessions.
source: The performance of mice quickly improved to an expert level, defined as fraction of correct trials >80%, within 3–6 sessions (4.18 ± 0.27 sessions, mean ± s.e.m., n = 17 mice; Figure 1E) by first increasing the hit rate, and then increasing the CR rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Mice learned to suppress their licking in response to a no-go cue, while preserving their licking in response to a go cue.
source: Therefore, mice learned to suppress their licking in response to a no-go cue, while preserving their licking in response to a go cue.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data showing changes in FA licking while hit licking remained stable.

claim: Muscimol injection into the Crus II decreased the hit rate compared with the saline control.
source: The muscimol injection decreased the hit rate compared with the saline control (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from muscimol injection experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Licking in hit trials was delayed and slower in muscimol injection sessions.
source: Moreover, licking in hit trials was delayed and slower in muscimol injection sessions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D), and licking in FA trials was also delayed by muscimol injection (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from muscimol injection experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-F.

claim: The Crus II contributes to the proper initiation and speed of conditioned licking.
source: These results indicate that the Crus II contributes to the proper initiation and speed of conditioned licking.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the muscimol injection experiments showing effects on licking behavior.

claim: In the Aldoc-tdTomato mouse line, AldC expression can be visualized in vivo as red tdTomato fluorescence.
source: In this mouse line, AldC expression can be visualized in vivo as red tdTomato fluorescence (Figure 2A and B, left); we have previously shown by immunohistochemistry that the expression of tdTomato precisely corresponds to that of AldC (Tsutsumi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 2A and B and a citation to Tsutsumi et al., 2015.

claim: CF signals were observed immediately after the cue onset and were robust during hit trials in AldC+ PCs.
source: CF signals were observed immediately after the cue onset and were robust during hit trials in AldC+ PCs (5+ AldC compartment; Figure 2D and E), whereas much smaller responses were observed in AldC− PCs (5− AldC compartment; Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The response pattern was clearly separated at the boundary of AldC expression.
source: This response pattern was clearly separated at the boundary of AldC expression (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The percentage of responsive ROIs in AldC+ compartments was higher for licking trials (hit and FA) than for non-licking trials (CR).
source: On average, the percentage of ROIs that respond during the early time window (0–0.5 s from cue onset) in AldC+ compartments was higher for licking trials (hit and FA) than for non-licking trials (CR), and scaled with lick rate (hit > FA; Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The percentage of responsive ROIs in AldC+ compartments during hit trials was significantly higher than that in AldC− compartments.
source: The percentage of responsive ROIs in AldC+ compartments during hit trials was significantly higher than that in AldC− compartments (Figure 2F), suggesting that CF inputs to AldC+ compartments are more relevant to motor behavior than those to AldC– compartments.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Differences in response probability were noted across the AldC boundaries for either or all of hit, FA, and CR trials.
source: Differences in response probability were noted across the AldC boundaries for either or all of hit, FA, and CR trials (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that the AldC expression boundaries have a close (≦ 100 µm) spatial correspondence with the CF functional boundaries.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of response probability across AldC boundaries shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mean coincidence rates across animals were as high as 90% in 7+/6−, 5−/5+, and 5+/5a− boundaries.
source: Mean coincidence rates across animals were as high as 90% in 7+/6−, 5−/5+, and 5+/5a− boundaries (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C), indicating that unbiased clustering of ROIs on the basis of their responses corresponds to separation using AldC expression at cellular resolution at these boundaries, but more broadly tuned in the other boundaries.
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C.

claim: CF signals in a lateral AldC+ compartment (7+) during hit trials were precisely time-locked to sensory cues followed by suppression.
source: First, CF signals in a lateral AldC+ compartment (7+) during hit trials were precisely time-locked to sensory cues followed by suppression (Figure 3B, top), whereas those in a medial AldC+ compartment (5a+) persisted long after the cues (Figure 3B, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Task-related CF signals were distinct across AldC expression boundaries at lateral AldC compartments (7+/6−), whereas there was less difference across medial AldC compartments (5a+/4b−).
source: Second, task-related CF signals were distinct across AldC expression boundaries at lateral AldC compartments (7+/6−), whereas there was less difference across medial AldC compartments (5a+/4b−; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Task-related CF signals were graded in extent depending on lick rate (hit > FA) in the medial AldC compartments (5a+ and 4b−).
source: Finally, task-related CF signals were graded in extent depending on lick rate (hit > FA) in the medial AldC compartments (5a+ and 4b−), whereas there was a distinct difference between responses to go and no-go cues in the lateral AldC compartment (7+; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The lateral and medial Crus II were separable at the boundary of 5−/5+.
source: On the basis of these task-related CF signals in individual compartments, the lateral and medial Crus II were separable at the boundary of 5−/5+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), where complete separation of the functional clusters and the correlation matrix was observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of CF signals across compartments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The percentage of ROIs responding during hit trials was higher for the medial AldC compartments than for the lateral AldC compartments, irrespective of AldC expression profile.
source: We found that the percentage of ROIs responding during hit trials was higher for the medial AldC compartments than for the lateral AldC compartments, irrespective of AldC expression profile (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The percentage was graded depending on the lick rate in the medial AldC compartments (hit > FA).
source: The percentage was graded depending on the lick rate in the medial AldC compartments (hit > FA; Figure 3C and D), whereas that in the lateral AldC compartments was equal for all trial types (Figure 3C) or pronounced in FA trials (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The percentage of responding ROIs for CR trials was higher for the lateral than for the medial AldC compartments, again irrespective of AldC expression.
source: The percentage of responding ROIs for CR trials was higher for the lateral than for the medial AldC compartments, again irrespective of AldC expression (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: CF inputs to the lateral AldC compartments report task onsets regardless of motor behavior, whereas those to the medial AldC compartments reflect motor behavior.
source: These results suggest that CF inputs to the lateral AldC compartments report task onsets regardless of motor behavior, whereas those to the medial AldC compartments reflect motor behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the quantitative analysis of CF signals across lateral and medial compartments.

claim: Slight decreases in CF signals were found during the pre-cue (−1 to 0 s from cue) period in the 5+ compartment.
source: We found slight decreases in CF signals during the pre-cue (−1 to 0 s from cue) period in the 5+ compartment (effect size = 0.18; Supplementary file 1), early increase (0 to 0.5 s from cue) in CF signals in all the AldC compartments, and secondary increase (2nd; 0.5 to 1 s from cue) in all the medial AldC compartments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and effect size reported in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Early increase (0 to 0.5 s from cue) in CF signals was found in all the AldC compartments.
source: We found slight decreases in CF signals during the pre-cue (−1 to 0 s from cue) period in the 5+ compartment (effect size = 0.18; Supplementary file 1), early increase (0 to 0.5 s from cue) in CF signals in all the AldC compartments, and secondary increase (2nd; 0.5 to 1 s from cue) in all the medial AldC compartments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Secondary increase (2nd; 0.5 to 1 s from cue) in CF signals was found in all the medial AldC compartments.
source: We found slight decreases in CF signals during the pre-cue (−1 to 0 s from cue) period in the 5+ compartment (effect size = 0.18; Supplementary file 1), early increase (0 to 0.5 s from cue) in CF signals in all the AldC compartments, and secondary increase (2nd; 0.5 to 1 s from cue) in all the medial AldC compartments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pre-cue decreases and early and secondary increases in CF signals can co-exist, even in single dendrites at single trials.
source: These pre-cue decreases and early and secondary increases in CF signals can co-exist, even in single dendrites at single trials (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-trial calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: A decrease in CF signals in the lateral AldC compartments and an increase in the 5a− compartment at late timing (1.2 to 2.2 s from lick onset) during hit trials was revealed by alignment of CF signals at lick onset.
source: Alignment of CF signals at lick onset in task-related and non-task-related lick bouts revealed a decrease in CF signals in the lateral AldC compartments and an increase in the 5a− compartment at late timing (1.2 to 2.2 s from lick onset) during hit trials (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by lick-aligned calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Pre-cue decreases in CF signals in the 5+ compartment were significantly correlated with the initiation of licking in the trial.
source: We found that the pre-cue decreases in CF signals in the 5+ compartment (medial AldC+) were significantly correlated with the initiation of licking in the trial (p=0.04; Figure 4B), indicating their role in motor preparation.
evidence: This claim is supported by GLMM analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Lick initiation was significantly delayed when there were pre-cue decreases in CF signals in the 5− compartment in the trial.
source: We found that lick initiation was significantly delayed when there were pre-cue decreases in CF signals in the 5− compartment in the trial (p=0.03; Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of lick latency distributions shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Pre-cue decreases in CF signals in the 5− compartment were significantly correlated with longer lick latency.
source: We also built a separate GLMM to fit single trial population averaged ΔF/F in single AldC compartments during the pre-cue time window using lick latency in the trial, and found that pre-cue decreases in CF signals in the 5− compartment were significantly correlated with longer lick latency (p=0.02; Figure 4D), indicating the role of CF inputs to this compartment in an animal's attention to the task.
evidence: This claim is supported by GLMM analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Early increases in CF signals in the 6−, 5+, and 5a− compartments were significantly correlated with lick initiation.
source: We found that early increases in CF signals in the 6−, 5+, and 5a− compartments were significantly correlated with lick initiation (p=0.03, 0.01, and 0.02; Figure 5B, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by GLMM analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Early increases in CF signals in the 6− and 5− compartments (lateral AldC−) were significantly correlated with no-go cues.
source: Go and no-go cues were oppositely represented in the lateral and medial AldC compartments: early increases in CF signals in the 6− and 5− compartments (lateral AldC−) were significantly correlated with no-go cues (p=0.0008 and 0.01), whereas those in the 5+, 5a+, and 4b− compartments (medial AldC) were significantly correlated with go cues (p=2 × 10−7, 7 × 10−5, and 0.02; Figure 5B, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by GLMM analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Early increases in CF signals in the 5+, 5a+, and 4b− compartments (medial AldC) were significantly correlated with go cues.
source: Go and no-go cues were oppositely represented in the lateral and medial AldC compartments: early increases in CF signals in the 6− and 5− compartments (lateral AldC−) were significantly correlated with no-go cues (p=0.0008 and 0.01), whereas those in the 5+, 5a+, and 4b− compartments (medial AldC) were significantly correlated with go cues (p=2 × 10−7, 7 × 10−5, and 0.02; Figure 5B, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by GLMM analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The presence of early CF signals in the 5+ compartment was significantly correlated with shorter lick latency.
source: We found that the presence of early CF signals in the 5+ compartment was significantly correlated with shorter lick latency (p=3 × 10−5; Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of lick latency distributions shown in Figure 5C.

claim: GLMM fitting revealed significantly negative correlation between early CF signals and lick latency in the 5+, 5a−, and 4b− compartments (medial AldC).
source: Indeed, GLMM fitting of single trial population averaged ΔF/F in single AldC compartments during licking trials using lick latency revealed significantly negative correlation in the 5+, 5a−, and 4b− compartments (medial AldC); lick latency was shorter with more CF signals in these AldC compartments (p=0.02, 0.0008, and 0.05; Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by GLMM analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The presence of early CF signals in the 5+ compartment was significantly correlated with faster lick rate.
source: We compared instantaneous lick rate in the licking trials with or without early CF signals in an AldC compartment, and found that the presence of early CF signals in the 5+ compartment was significantly correlated with faster lick rate (p=4 × 10−6; Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of lick rate shown in Figure 5E.

claim: GLMM fitting revealed a significant positive correlation between early CF signals and lick rate in the 5+ and 5a+ compartments (medial AldC+).
source: GLMM fitting of single trial population averaged ΔF/F in single AldC compartments during licking trials (as in Figure 5D) revealed a significant positive correlation in the 5+ and 5a+ compartments (medial AldC+): lick rate was faster with more CF signals in these compartments (p=0.01 and 0.02; Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by GLMM analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Early increases in CF signals reflect lick initiation and context discrimination, and licking is shorter in latency and faster when CF signals show early increases in the medial AldC compartments.
source: In summary, early increases in CF signals reflect lick initiation and context discrimination, and licking is shorter in latency and faster when CF signals show early increases in the medial AldC compartments.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the analyses in Figure 5.

claim: The presence of secondary increases in CF signals in the 5a− compartment was significantly correlated with faster licking.
source: We found that the presence of secondary increases in CF signals in the 5a− compartment was significantly correlated with faster licking (p=0.02; Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of lick rate shown in Figure 6B.

claim: GLMM fitting revealed significantly positive correlation between secondary CF signals and lick rate in the 5+, 5a−, and 4b− compartments (medial AldC).
source: GLMM fitting of single trial population averaged ΔF/F in single AldC compartments using the lick rate of the first lick bout in the single licking trial revealed significantly positive correlation in the 5+, 5a−, and 4b− compartments (medial AldC); lick rate was faster with more CF signals in these AldC compartments (p=0.04, 0.04, and 0.008; Figure 6C), indicating the importance of the medial Crus II for speed of licking.
evidence: This claim is supported by GLMM analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Decreases in CF signals in all the lateral AldC compartments and in the 5+ compartment, as well as increases in the 5a− compartment, were significantly correlated with the presence of reward.
source: We found that decreases in CF signals in all the lateral AldC compartments and in the 5+ compartment, as well as increases in the 5a− compartment, were significantly correlated with the presence of reward (7+, p=0.0002; 6−, p=3 × 10−12; 6+, p=1 × 10−12; 5−, p=2 × 10−7; 5+, p=0.0008; 5a−, p=3 × 10−5; Figure 7C), indicating that these signals reflect positive reward outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by GLMM analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: CF signals in the AldC+ compartments show graded activity after sensory cues, reflecting the speed and duration of motor behavior.
source: CF signals in the AldC+ compartments show graded activity after sensory cues, reflecting the speed and duration of motor behavior, whereas those in the AldC− compartments show similar activity in response to sensory cues regardless of the presence and absence of motor behavior, and therefore represent a sensory response.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data across multiple figures.

claim: CF signals in the AldC− compartments show similar activity in response to sensory cues regardless of the presence and absence of motor behavior, and therefore represent a sensory response.
source: CF signals in the AldC+ compartments show graded activity after sensory cues, reflecting the speed and duration of motor behavior, whereas those in the AldC− compartments show similar activity in response to sensory cues regardless of the presence and absence of motor behavior, and therefore represent a sensory response.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data across multiple figures.

claim: CF signals in the lateral Crus II represent a sensory response, whereas those in the medial Crus II represent motor behavior.
source: CF signals in the lateral AldC compartments represent a sensory response, whereas those in the medial AldC compartments represent motor behavior.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data across multiple figures.

claim: Pre-cue decreases represent motor preparation.
source: These spatially segregated CF signals represent the behavior of mice in a temporally organized manner: pre-cue decreases represent motor preparation; early increases represent motor initiation, timing, and speed, and go/no-go discrimination; secondary increases represent motor speed; and late decreases represent positive reward outcomes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Early increases represent motor initiation, timing, and speed, and go/no-go discrimination.
source: These spatially segregated CF signals represent the behavior of mice in a temporally organized manner: pre-cue decreases represent motor preparation; early increases represent motor initiation, timing, and speed, and go/no-go discrimination; secondary increases represent motor speed; and late decreases represent positive reward outcomes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: Secondary increases represent motor speed.
source: These spatially segregated CF signals represent the behavior of mice in a temporally organized manner: pre-cue decreases represent motor preparation; early increases represent motor initiation, timing, and speed, and go/no-go discrimination; secondary increases represent motor speed; and late decreases represent positive reward outcomes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Late decreases represent positive reward outcomes.
source: These spatially segregated CF signals represent the behavior of mice in a temporally organized manner: pre-cue decreases represent motor preparation; early increases represent motor initiation, timing, and speed, and go/no-go discrimination; secondary increases represent motor speed; and late decreases represent positive reward outcomes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: Lesions of inferior olivary subnuclei have been reported to cause specific behavioral deficits in cats.
source: In accordance with our observation of diverse task-related CF signals across AldC compartments (Figure 8), lesions of inferior olivary subnuclei have been reported to cause specific behavioral deficits in cats (Horn et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Horn et al., 2010.

claim: Group I compartments (7+, 6+, and 5+) are innervated by CFs originating from the principal olive and neighboring areas.
source: According to a grouping of cerebellar modules on the basis of a detailed tracing study (Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004), group I compartments (7+, 6+, and 5+) are innervated by CFs originating from the principal olive and neighboring areas.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004.

claim: Group I compartments receive inputs from the cerebral cortex via the nuclei in the mesodiencephalic junction, including the red nucleus, area parafascicularis prerubralis, and nucleus of Darkschewitsch.
source: These compartments receive inputs from the cerebral cortex via the nuclei in the mesodiencephalic junction, including the red nucleus, area parafascicularis prerubralis, and nucleus of Darkschewitsch (Stuesse and Newman, 1990; Swenson and Castro, 1983; Veazey and Severin, 1982).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Stuesse and Newman, 1990; Swenson and Castro, 1983; Veazey and Severin, 1982.

claim: Perioral tactile information is directly conveyed by a pathway from the periphery to the Crus II via the mesodiencephalic junction and inferior olive.
source: Furthermore, a recent study showed that perioral tactile information is directly conveyed by a pathway from the periphery to the Crus II via the mesodiencephalic junction and inferior olive (Kubo et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kubo et al., 2018.

claim: Group IV compartments (6− and 5−) receive CF inputs from the dorsomedial group of the principal olive and the medial part of the dorsal accessory olive.
source: Group IV compartments (6− and 5−) receive CF inputs from the dorsomedial group of the principal olive and the medial part of the dorsal accessory olive, which receive somatosensory inputs from the spinal cord, dorsal column nuclei, and trigeminal nucleus (Molinari et al., 1996; Swenson and Castro, 1983).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Molinari et al., 1996; Swenson and Castro, 1983.

claim: Group II (5a+, 4b+, and 4+) and III compartments (5a− and 4b−) are innervated by CFs from the medial subnuclei and medial accessory olive.
source: Group II (5a+, 4b+, and 4+) and III compartments (5a− and 4b−) are innervated by CFs from the medial subnuclei and medial accessory olive, which receive somatosensory inputs from the spinal cord as well as vestibular and collicular inputs (Akaike, 1992; Boesten and Voogd, 1975; Brown et al., 1977; Swenson and Castro, 1983).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Akaike, 1992; Boesten and Voogd, 1975; Brown et al., 1977; Swenson and Castro, 1983.

claim: Only PCs in the lateral part of group I and IV compartments (7+, 6−, and 6+) project to the dentate nucleus.
source: In terms of outputs, only PCs in the lateral part of group I and IV compartments (7+, 6−, and 6+) project to the dentate nucleus (Sugihara, 2011), which in turn projects back to a wide range of brain regions, including the motor and association cortices (Dum and Strick, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sugihara, 2011 and Dum and Strick, 2003.

claim: The dentate nucleus projects back to a wide range of brain regions, including the motor and association cortices.
source: In terms of outputs, only PCs in the lateral part of group I and IV compartments (7+, 6−, and 6+) project to the dentate nucleus (Sugihara, 2011), which in turn projects back to a wide range of brain regions, including the motor and association cortices (Dum and Strick, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dum and Strick, 2003.

claim: PCs located in the medial part of group I and IV compartments (5− and 5+) and those in group II/III compartments (5a−, 5a+, 4b−, 4b+, and 4+) project to the sensorimotor cortex via interpositus and fastigial nuclei.
source: PCs located in the medial part of group I and IV compartments (5− and 5+) and those in group II/III compartments (5a−, 5a+, 4b−, 4b+, and 4+) project to the sensorimotor cortex via interpositus and fastigial nuclei, respectively (Sugihara, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sugihara, 2011.

claim: AldC+ PCs have a lower simple spike rate and a higher complex spike rate than AldC− PCs, which are dependent on co-expressing TRPC3 subtypes.
source: Previous studies have suggested several functional differences between AldC+ and AldC− PCs: (i) AldC+ PCs have a lower simple spike rate and a higher complex spike rate than AldC− PCs, which are dependent on co-expressing TRPC3 subtypes (Zhou et al., 2014);
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2014.

claim: Coupling between simple spikes and complex spikes is enhanced in AldC+ PCs.
source: (ii) coupling between simple spikes and complex spikes is enhanced in AldC+ PCs (Tang et al., 2017);
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tang et al., 2017.

claim: At the population level, CF inputs to AldC+ and AldC− compartments are separately and precisely synchronized at the cellular resolution.
source: (iv) at the population level, CF inputs to AldC+ and AldC− compartments are separately and precisely synchronized at the cellular resolution (Tsutsumi et al., 2015);
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tsutsumi et al., 2015.

claim: More AldC+ PCs than AldC− PCs receive motor-related CF inputs.
source: In the present study, we found that more AldC+ PCs than AldC− PCs receive motor-related CF inputs (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Complex spike firing has been shown to be synchronized exclusively within AldC compartments in the lateral Crus II, whereas it can be synchronized across AldC compartments in the medial Crus II.

claim: CF inputs to the lateral Crus II might represent sensory saliency and/or attention signals, which could be conveyed via the dentate nucleus to be used for higher-order processing in the association cortices.
source: These findings imply distinct behavioral functions of CF inputs to the lateral and medial cerebellum: CF inputs to the lateral Crus II might represent sensory saliency and/or attention signals, which could be conveyed via the dentate nucleus to be used for higher-order processing in the association cortices, whereas CF inputs to the medial Crus II could control motor behavior online (Welsh et al., 1995) by indirect projections, via the interpositus and fastigial nuclei, to either the motor cortex or brainstem motor neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings based on anatomical connectivity.

claim: CF inputs to the medial Crus II could control motor behavior online by indirect projections, via the interpositus and fastigial nuclei, to either the motor cortex or brainstem motor neurons.

claim: The anticipatory decrease in CF signals could reflect ramping-up activity in cerebellar nuclei via nucleo-olivary inhibitory projections.
source: Given the anticipatory ramping-up activity in dentate nuclear neurons in monkeys representing timing prediction (Ashmore and Sommer, 2013; Ohmae et al., 2017), as well as fastigial/dentate nuclear neurons in mice representing motor preparation (Chabrol et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2018), the anticipatory decreases in CF signals that we observed could reflect ramping-up activity in these cerebellar nuclei via nucleo-olivary inhibitory projections (Hesslow, 1986).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on citations to Ashmore and Sommer, 2013; Ohmae et al., 2017; Chabrol et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2018; Hesslow, 1986.
